claim: 160,987 publicly available Eubacteria genomes were screened for the presence of AME genes.
source: 160,987 publicly available Eubacteria genomes were screened for the presence of AME genes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genomes screened in the Results section.

claim: A total of 46,053 AME genes were detected in 38,523 genomes.
source: A total of 46,053 AME genes were detected in 38,523 genomes (i.e. about one quarter of the genomes screened).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of detected AME genes and genomes.

claim: About 25% of sequenced bacteria carry AME genes.
source: We find that AME genes display a very ubiquitous pattern: about 25% of sequenced bacteria carry AME genes.
evidence: The abstract states this prevalence based on the screening results.

claim: AME bacteria were sequenced from all the continents except Antarctica.
source: These bacteria were sequenced from all the continents (except Antarctica) and terrestrial biomes, and belong to a wide number of phyla.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the geographical distribution of sampled bacteria.

claim: Aminoglycoside consumption has little impact on the prevalence of AME-gene-carrying bacteria in European countries between 1997 and 2018.
source: By focusing on European countries between 1997 and 2018, we show that aminoglycoside consumption has little impact on the prevalence of AME-gene-carrying bacteria, whereas most variation in prevalence is observed among biomes.
evidence: The abstract summarizes findings from statistical modeling of European data.

claim: Most variation in AME bacteria prevalence is observed among biomes.
source: By focusing on European countries between 1997 and 2018, we show that aminoglycoside consumption has little impact on the prevalence of AME-gene-carrying bacteria, whereas most variation in prevalence is observed among biomes.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on analysis of European data.

claim: Soil, wildlife, and human samples appear to be central to understand the exchanges of AME genes between different ecological contexts.
source: We further analyze the resemblance of resistome compositions across biomes: soil, wildlife, and human samples appear to be central to understand the exchanges of AME genes between different ecological contexts.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on network analysis of resistome compositions.

claim: Antibiotic resistance is a persistent global public health problem that has increased over the last decades.
source: Antibiotic resistance (AR) is a persistent global public health problem that has increased over the last decades, with resistances spreading faster and faster after antibiotic introduction in clinical use (Witzany et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: The introduction cites a reference to support this statement about AR trends.

claim: Resistances are spreading faster and faster after antibiotic introduction in clinical use.
source: Antibiotic resistance (AR) is a persistent global public health problem that has increased over the last decades, with resistances spreading faster and faster after antibiotic introduction in clinical use (Witzany et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Witzany et al., 2020.

claim: First concerns about infections by antibiotic resistant bacteria were formulated in the 1940s.
source: Although first concerns about infections by antibiotic resistant bacteria (AR bacteria) were formulated in the 1940s, the discovery and development of new antibiotics allowed for treatment substitutions (Podolsky, 2018)⁠ during the first decades of antibiotic use.
evidence: The introduction cites Podolsky, 2018 to support this historical claim.

claim: The discovery and development of new antibiotics allowed for treatment substitutions during the first decades of antibiotic use.
source: Although first concerns about infections by antibiotic resistant bacteria (AR bacteria) were formulated in the 1940s, the discovery and development of new antibiotics allowed for treatment substitutions (Podolsky, 2018)⁠ during the first decades of antibiotic use.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Podolsky, 2018.

claim: The discovery and design of new antibiotics had become more and more difficult.
source: In parallel, the discovery and design of new antibiotics had become more and more difficult (Livermore et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Livermore et al., 2011.

claim: In 2019, around 1.25 million deaths were directly attributable to bacterial antimicrobial resistance.
source: A recent review (Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022) evaluated that in 2019, around 1.25 million deaths were directly attributable to bacterial antimicrobial resistance.
evidence: The statement cites a specific review that evaluated mortality from antimicrobial resistance.

claim: Antibiotic consumption and its abuses have been historically and repeatedly pointed out as the major cause of AR genes propagation.
source: Antibiotic consumption and its abuses have been historically and repeatedly pointed out as the major cause of AR genes propagation (O'Neill, 2014; Podolsky, 2018; Schrijver et al., 2018): the frequency of AR increases in bacteria communities under the selective pressure of antibiotics.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The frequency of AR increases in bacteria communities under the selective pressure of antibiotics.
source: Antibiotic consumption and its abuses have been historically and repeatedly pointed out as the major cause of AR genes propagation (O'Neill, 2014; Podolsky, 2018; Schrijver et al., 2018): the frequency of AR increases in bacteria communities under the selective pressure of antibiotics.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle following citations about AR propagation.

claim: A meta-analysis over 243 studies found a positive correlation between antibiotic consumption and presence of AR.
source: This perception of the factors driving AR spread and its associated policies still prevail nowadays: for example, a meta-analysis over 243 studies found a positive correlation between antibiotic consumption and presence of AR (Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement cites a specific meta-analysis by Bell et al., 2014.

claim: A drastic reduction in sulfonamide consumption in the United Kingdom during the 1990s was not followed by a decrease in prevalence of sulfonamide-resistant Escherichia coli.
source: However, even if antibiotic consumption decreases in most developed countries, AR does not always follow the same path: for example, a drastic reduction in sulfonamide consumption in the United Kingdom during the 1990s was not followed by a decrease in prevalence of sulfonamide-resistant Escherichia coli (Enne et al., 2004)⁠.
evidence: The statement cites Enne et al., 2004 as evidence for this specific example.

claim: Antibiotic consumption does not seem to be the only factor maintaining AR in pathogenic bacteria communities.
source: Antibiotic consumption therefore does not seem to be the only factor maintaining AR in pathogenic bacteria communities.
evidence: This inference is drawn from the example of sulfonamide resistance persistence.

claim: Integrative studies identifying large-scale trends in AR are lacking.
source: Indeed, although the impact of human activities on the circulation and spread of AR genes is now well documented through the accumulation of specific examples, integrative studies identifying large-scale trends are lacking and this absence of general view has been pinpointed as a gap in our knowledge of drivers of antimicrobial resistance (Holmes et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement cites Holmes et al., 2016 to support this claim about gaps in knowledge.

claim: AR genes have probably always been natural members of the gene pools of environmental microbial communities.
source: Though data in natural ecosystems remain scarce, AR genes have probably always been natural members of the gene pools of environmental microbial communities (D'Costa et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to D'Costa et al., 2011.

claim: Natural ecosystems may contribute to the spread of AR, both as sources and as vectors of propagation.
source: Natural ecosystems may contribute to the spread of AR, both as sources and as vectors of propagation (Bengtsson-Palme et al., 2018; Berendonk et al., 2015; Marti et al., 2014)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aminoglycosides are antibiotics that bind to the 30 S subunit of prokaryotic ribosomes and thus inhibit protein synthesis.
source: Aminoglycosides are antibiotics that bind to the 30 S subunit of prokaryotic ribosomes and thus inhibit protein synthesis (Mingeot-Leclercq et al., 1999)⁠.
evidence: The statement describes the mechanism of action and cites Mingeot-Leclercq et al., 1999.

claim: Streptomycin was first introduced in 1944 and was successful against tuberculosis.
source: This antibiotic class was first introduced in 1944 with the successful use of streptomycin against tuberculosis, and the first antibiotic able to fight Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: The manuscript provides historical information about streptomycin introduction.

claim: Streptomycin was the first antibiotic able to fight Gram-negative bacteria.
source: This antibiotic class was first introduced in 1944 with the successful use of streptomycin against tuberculosis, and the first antibiotic able to fight Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: The manuscript states this historical fact about streptomycin.

claim: The emergence of resistant strains, combined with the requirement of administration by injection and possible nephro- and ototoxicity has reduced the use of aminoglycosides in therapies.
source: However, the emergence of resistant strains during the following years, combined with the requirement of administration by injection and possible nephro- and ototoxicity has reduced the use of aminoglycosides in therapies (Murray and Murray, 1991)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Murray and Murray, 1991.

claim: Aminoglycosides are only used in humans as a second-line or last-resort treatment for Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Nowadays, these drugs are only used in humans as a second-line or last-resort treatment for Gram-negative bacteria (Garneau-Tsodikova and Labby, 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Garneau-Tsodikova and Labby, 2016.

claim: Aminoglycosides remain frequently used in agriculture and veterinary medicine.
source: However, they remain frequently used in agriculture and veterinary medicine (European Medicines Agency, 2019)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to European Medicines Agency, 2019.

claim: In 2015, aminoglycosides represented 3.5% of the total sales of antimicrobials for farm animals.
source: As an example, in 2015, aminoglycosides still represented 3.5% of the total sales of antimicrobials for farm animals, and they are still important drugs for some pathologies, for example post-weaning diarrhoea in pigs (van Duijkeren et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement cites van Duijkeren et al., 2019 for this specific statistic.

claim: In Denmark, 85% of Salmonella spp. serovar Kentucky isolated in turkeys are not susceptible to aminoglycosides.
source: Thus, aminoglycoside resistance is still highly prevalent among farm animals: in Denmark, 85% of Salmonella spp. serovar Kentucky isolated in turkeys are not susceptible to aminoglycosides, and in Italy, up to 67% of E. coli samples are resistant to at least one aminoglycoside drug (van Duijkeren et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement cites van Duijkeren et al., 2019 for this specific prevalence data.

claim: In Italy, up to 67% of E. coli samples are resistant to at least one aminoglycoside drug.
source: Thus, aminoglycoside resistance is still highly prevalent among farm animals: in Denmark, 85% of Salmonella spp. serovar Kentucky isolated in turkeys are not susceptible to aminoglycosides, and in Italy, up to 67% of E. coli samples are resistant to at least one aminoglycoside drug (van Duijkeren et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement cites van Duijkeren et al., 2019 for this specific prevalence data.

claim: Most aminoglycosides originate from soil-dwelling bacteria.
source: Moreover, since most aminoglycosides originate from soil-dwelling bacteria, there are at least three ecological contexts (hospitals, farms, and soil) in which aminoglycoside resistance can evolve and spread to cause public health issues.
evidence: The manuscript states this as background knowledge about aminoglycoside origins.

claim: There are three main mechanisms of aminoglycoside resistance: decrease in drug uptake and/or increase in drug efflux; drug inactivating enzymes; and modification of the drug target.
source: The three main mechanisms of aminoglycoside resistance are (Garneau-Tsodikova and Labby, 2016)⁠: (i) decrease in drug uptake (through modifications of membrane permeability or of the peri-membrane ion gradient) and/or increase in drug efflux (through efflux pump activation); (ii) drug inactivating enzymes; and (iii) modification of the drug target, for example by point mutations in the genes coding for ribosomal small subunit (Finken et al., 1993; Sander et al., 1995; Toivonen et al., 1999)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations describing resistance mechanisms.

claim: AMEs represent the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance in clinical isolates.
source: AMEs represent the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance in clinical isolates and are well characterized biochemically (Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010.

claim: AMEs are well characterized biochemically.
source: AMEs represent the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance in clinical isolates and are well characterized biochemically (Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010.

claim: AMEs emerged several times during evolution.
source: However, AMEs emerged several times during evolution (see e.g. Salipante and Hall, 2003 for AAC(6') enzymes), so biochemical nomenclatures do not reflect the evolutionary history of any class of AMEs.
evidence: The statement cites Salipante and Hall, 2003 as an example of multiple emergence events.

claim: Biochemical nomenclatures do not reflect the evolutionary history of any class of AMEs.
source: However, AMEs emerged several times during evolution (see e.g. Salipante and Hall, 2003 for AAC(6') enzymes), so biochemical nomenclatures do not reflect the evolutionary history of any class of AMEs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fact that AMEs emerged multiple times.

claim: Many AME genes are carried by mobile genetic elements.
source: Finally, many AME genes are carried by mobile genetic elements, which give them the potential to be transmitted both vertically and horizontally (Davies, 1983)⁠.

source: They represent today a major threat for the treatment of multidrug-resistant bacteria, notably Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Labby and Garneau-Tsodikova, 2013)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Labby and Garneau-Tsodikova, 2013.

claim: Published sequences of AMEs and genes coding for AMEs had been previously grouped in 27 clusters of homologous genes.
source: Published sequences of AMEs and genes coding for AMEs had been previously grouped in 27 clusters of homologous genes (CHGs), each containing sequences of genes and proteins very likely to share a common ancestor (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodology used to define CHGs.

source: Moreover, whereas 23.9% of all the genomes in our dataset carried at least one AME gene, this proportion decreases to 16.3% across the least sampled species making up 50% of the dataset, and even to 10.9% across the species making up 10% of the dataset.

claim: Three main ecological modules were found in the resistome network: (1) clinical, farms, human, and agricultural samples; (2) soil, human habitat, waste, sludge, and freshwater; (3) domestic animals and wild plants and animals.
source: Based on the Louvain clustering algorithm, we found three main ecological modules in this network, clustered by their composition in CHGs: (1) clinical, farms, human, and agricultural samples; (2) soil, human habitat, waste, sludge, and freshwater; (3) domestic animals and wild plants and animals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of network clustering analysis.

claim: Wild plants and animals have the highest betweenness centrality in the resistome network.
source: In this network of resistome compositions, wild plants and animals have the highest betweenness centrality (i.e. it is an intermediate in 14 shortest paths in the network), followed by the human habitat (8 shortest paths), soil (7 shortest paths), and human samples (3 shortest paths).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific network centrality measures.

claim: Soil has the highest degree centrality in the resistome network.
source: But degree centrality is actually highest for soil (i.e. it shares connections with 7 other biomes), followed by wild plants and animals and human samples (6 connections each), and by agrosystems and farms (5 connections each).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific network centrality measures.

claim: Resistome resemblance is significantly, positively correlated with bacteria community composition similarity for module 1 (clinical, farms, human, and agricultural samples).

claim: Functional diversity increases with the number of resistance genes carried by a genome.
source: Using the resistance spectra inferred from Feldgarden et al., 2019⁠, two classical functional dissimilarity indices (functional dispersion, FDis, and Rao's quadratic entropy, RaoQE) indicated that the functional diversity increases, that is resistance spectrum widens, with the number of resistance genes carried by a genome (FDis, linear regression, R2=0.756, p<2.2.10–16 and RaoQE, linear regression, R2=0.746, p<2.2.10–16).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results from linear regression.

claim: The increase in functional diversity occurs at a higher rate than expected under the hypothesis of a random assortment of AME genes among genomes.
source: More importantly, these increases occur at a higher rate than expected under the hypothesis of a random assortment of AME genes among genomes, both for FDis (permutation test, 500 perms., p=1.2.10–3) and for RaoQE (permutation test, 500 perms., p=6.7.10–3).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific permutation test results.

claim: 15,374 AME genes were detected to be associated with MGE conferring intergenomic mobility.
source: Among the 46,053 AME genes detected in the initial screen, 15,374 were detected to be associated with MGE conferring intergenomic mobility (plasmids, prophages, or ICEs), and 9640 were detected to be associated with a MGE conferring intragenomic mobility (integrons or transposable elements).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of genes associated with MGEs.

claim: 9640 AME genes were detected to be associated with a MGE conferring intragenomic mobility.
source: Among the 46,053 AME genes detected in the initial screen, 15,374 were detected to be associated with MGE conferring intergenomic mobility (plasmids, prophages, or ICEs), and 9640 were detected to be associated with a MGE conferring intragenomic mobility (integrons or transposable elements).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of genes associated with MGEs.

claim: 7277 AME genes were detected to be associated with both intergenomic and intragenomic mobility MGEs.
source: A total of 7277 genes were detected to be associated with both at the same time.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of genes associated with both types of MGEs.

claim: The proportion of genes associated with MGEs is very heterogeneous between CHGs, covering the full range from 0% to 100%.
source: The proportion of genes associated with MGEs is actually very heterogeneous between CHGs, covering the full range from 0% to 100% (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 7.

claim: The increase rate of functional diversity is significantly higher than expected under random assortment for genes associated with MGEs conferring intergenomic mobility.
source: Yet, the increase rate is significantly higher than expected under the hypothesis of random assortment for genes associated with MGEs conferring intergenomic mobility (permutation test, 500 perms., p=1.2.10–3 for FDis, p=1.2.10–3 for RaoQE), whatever the source used to infer resistance spectra.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific permutation test results.

claim: The probability for an AME gene to undergo intragenomic replication is at least 10 times higher when associated with MGEs.
source: The probability for an AME gene to undergo intragenomic replication is at least 10 times higher when associated with MGEs, under the hypothesis of random MGE-gene assortment (permutation test, 500 perms., p=1.2.10–3).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results from permutation tests.

claim: About one quarter of bacteria screened carry a gene known to provide resistance to aminoglycosides.
source: In this study, we defined and screened 27 clusters of genes encoding resistance to aminoglycosides across more than 160,000 genomes spread across phylogeny, ecology, geography, and time. About one quarter of these bacteria were found to carry a gene known to provide resistance to aminoglycosides.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding in the Discussion.

claim: The lowest prevalence of AME bacteria found in a biome was 9%.
source: This very high prevalence of aminoglycoside resistance is likely biased by the much higher availability of genomic data for human, clinical, and agriculture isolates. Yet, the lowest prevalence found in a biome was actually 9%, which is consistent with previous studies on genomic (Pal et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020) and metagenomic (Zhang et al., 2020)⁠ datasets sampled from multiple biomes.
evidence: The manuscript provides this specific prevalence value and cites supporting studies.

claim: Around 40% of the AR genes found were potentially mobile.
source: Around 40% of the AR genes found were potentially mobile, that is associated with plasmids, integrons, prophages, ICEs or transposons.
evidence: The manuscript provides this specific percentage.

claim: AME bacteria were found as early as 1905.
source: AME bacteria were found as early as 1905, that is nearly 40 years before the first aminoglycoside was isolated and identified as a potential antibacterial therapeutic agent.
evidence: The manuscript provides this specific temporal finding.

claim: Aminoglycosides are naturally produced by bacteria from the Streptomyces and Micromonospora genera.
source: This is not a surprise as aminoglycosides are naturally produced by bacteria from the Streptomyces and Micromonospora genera (Durand et al., 2019)⁠ and the selection pressure for the evolution of resistance genes existed long before the clinical use of aminoglycosides, as shown for other antibiotic resistance genes (D'Costa et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Durand et al., 2019 and D'Costa et al., 2011.

claim: The selection pressure for the evolution of resistance genes existed long before the clinical use of aminoglycosides.
source: This is not a surprise as aminoglycosides are naturally produced by bacteria from the Streptomyces and Micromonospora genera (Durand et al., 2019)⁠ and the selection pressure for the evolution of resistance genes existed long before the clinical use of aminoglycosides, as shown for other antibiotic resistance genes (D'Costa et al., 2011)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to D'Costa et al., 2011.

claim: AME bacteria prevalence has plateaued around 30% since the 1990s.
source: AME bacteria prevalence strongly increased between the 1940s and the 1980s, and has plateaued around 30% since the 1990s (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal trends and references Figure 4B.

claim: Reduction of antibiotic consumption and fighting antibiotic pollution have historically been the most common public health recommendation to control or reduce the spread of antibiotic resistance.
source: Reduction of antibiotic consumption and fighting antibiotic pollution have historically been the most common public health recommendation to control or reduce the spread of antibiotic resistance (see e.g. Mölstad et al., 2008; Sabuncu et al., 2009)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Mölstad et al., 2008 and Sabuncu et al., 2009.

claim: Selection is considered the major determinant in the emergence, accumulation, and propagation of resistance in evolutionary epidemiology.
source: The predominance of this recommendation is driven by the idea, in evolutionary epidemiology, that selection is the major determinant in the emergence, accumulation, and propagation of resistance (Blanquart et al., 2017; Spicknall et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Blanquart et al., 2017 and Spicknall et al., 2013.

claim: Correlative studies have linked antibiotic consumption levels and resistance prevalence, mainly in environments where antibiotic consumption is high such as hospitals or farms.
source: This idea is supported by correlative studies linking antibiotic consumption levels and resistance prevalence, mainly in environments where antibiotic consumption is high such as hospitals or farms (e.g. Goossens et al., 2005)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Goossens et al., 2005.

claim: Between 1997 and 2018 in Europe, aminoglycoside consumption is not the main factor explaining AME genes prevalence patterns.
source: Thus, independently of the biomes considered, our results show that between 1997 and 2018 in Europe, aminoglycoside consumption is not the main factor explaining AME genes prevalence patterns.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on statistical modeling.

claim: The average prevalence of bacteria carrying AACf1 was 1.5% in France and 18.1% in Austria between 1997 and 2018.
source: There are even in this dataset examples of low ARB prevalence occurring in countries with high antibiotics consumption: for example over the period, the average prevalence of bacteria carrying AACf1 was 1.5% in France and 18.1% in Austria, whereas these two countries consumed on average respectively 0.22 and 0.02 g per inhabitant/human-equivalent of aminoglycosides each year.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific prevalence data for these countries.

claim: France consumed on average 0.22 g per inhabitant/human-equivalent of aminoglycosides each year between 1997 and 2018.
source: There are even in this dataset examples of low ARB prevalence occurring in countries with high antibiotics consumption: for example over the period, the average prevalence of bacteria carrying AACf1 was 1.5% in France and 18.1% in Austria, whereas these two countries consumed on average respectively 0.22 and 0.02 g per inhabitant/human-equivalent of aminoglycosides each year.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific consumption data for France.

claim: Austria consumed on average 0.02 g per inhabitant/human-equivalent of aminoglycosides each year between 1997 and 2018.
source: There are even in this dataset examples of low ARB prevalence occurring in countries with high antibiotics consumption: for example over the period, the average prevalence of bacteria carrying AACf1 was 1.5% in France and 18.1% in Austria, whereas these two countries consumed on average respectively 0.22 and 0.02 g per inhabitant/human-equivalent of aminoglycosides each year.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific consumption data for Austria.

claim: Many AMEs might have evolved as adaptations to antibiotics produced in natural communities.
source: Additionally, several mechanisms can allow resistant strains to thrive even under decreasing antibiotic selection pressure. (i) Selective pressures on AR are multiple and man-made antimicrobial agents are just one of them. Many AMEs might have evolved as adaptations to antibiotics produced in natural communities, or as exaptations of metabolic enzymes selected for other functions (e.g. AACs from enzymes involved in the acetylation of ribosomal proteins, Rather, 1998).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Rather, 1998.

claim: AME genes can be maintained in populations by hitchhiking on other genes carried on the same MGE.
source: (ii) AME genes can be maintained in populations by hitchhiking on other genes (e.g. resistance to heavy metals, biocides) carried on the same MGE (Zhai et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Zhai et al., 2016.

claim: AR genes can be silenced in nonselective conditions and be reactivated in selective conditions only.
source: (iii) Carrying an AR gene is costly only if the gene is expressed, but AR genes can be silenced in nonselective conditions and be reactivated in selective conditions only (Kime et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Kime et al., 2019.

claim: Reducing aminoglycoside consumption is a necessary but not a sufficient measure to limit the propagation of antibiotic resistances.
source: The results of our integrated study strongly suggest that reducing aminoglycoside consumption is a necessary but not a sufficient measure to limit the propagation of antibiotic resistances and that complementary measures based on the reduction of other selection pressures (such as heavy metal pollution, Seiler and Berendonk, 2012) maintaining AR gene frequency should be implemented.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Human exchanges explain a significant part of the variation in the prevalence of AME bacteria for a higher number of CHGs than antibiotics consumption does.
source: In our dataset, human exchanges explain a significant part of the variation in the prevalence of AME bacteria for a higher number of CHGs than antibiotics consumption does.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on statistical modeling.

claim: AR bacteria can be carried over continents by plant and animal products exchanged through international trade.
source: Numerous examples of direct impact of human activities, outside of antibiotic use, on the emergence, retention, and propagation of AR have been documented: AR bacteria can be carried over continents by plant (Zurfluh et al., 2015)⁠ and animal products (Eltai et al., 2020; Le Hello et al., 2011)⁠, exchanged through international trade, as well as immigrants (Nellums et al., 2018)⁠ and travelers in general (e.g. Lepelletier et al., 2011⁠).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: AR bacteria can be carried by immigrants and travelers.
source: Numerous examples of direct impact of human activities, outside of antibiotic use, on the emergence, retention, and propagation of AR have been documented: AR bacteria can be carried over continents by plant (Zurfluh et al., 2015)⁠ and animal products (Eltai et al., 2020; Le Hello et al., 2011)⁠, exchanged through international trade, as well as immigrants (Nellums et al., 2018)⁠ and travelers in general (e.g. Lepelletier et al., 2011⁠).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The resemblance between resistomes depended more on the biomes in which they were sampled, than on their geographical location.
source: Not only did we find a wide diversity of AME genes outside of hospitals and farms, where antibiotics are the most consumed (see Figure 3), but differences between biomes explained most of the variance when the frequency of AR bacteria was modeled over time, space, and ecology. Across ecosystems (defined as the intersection of a biome and a geographical unit), we found that the resemblance between resistomes depended more on the biomes in which they were sampled, than on their geographical location.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on network analysis.

claim: AR genes are shared with 100% identity between soil bacteria and human pathogens.
source: Yet, consistent with Forsberg et al., 2012⁠ who found AR genes shared with 100% identity between soil bacteria and human pathogens, many AR genes were still shared between biomes, including between natural and anthropized biomes.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Forsberg et al., 2012.

claim: Fauna and flora and soil have the highest measures of centrality in the network of resistomes.
source: Additionally, the study of certain biomes seems crucial to understand the spread of AR. Indeed, in the network of resistomes, 'fauna and flora' and 'soil' have the highest measures of centrality, which suggests that these two biomes are involved in most events of AME gene transfer across ecology (either as an origin or as a destination).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on network analysis.

claim: Natural ecosystems have been suggested to constitute reservoirs for AR genes originating from hospitals.
source: This could be explained by both antibiotics and AR genes transferred from humans and anthropized habitat to natural ecosystems. Natural ecosystems have actually been suggested to constitute reservoirs for AR genes originating from hospitals (see e.g. Baquero et al., 2009; Tripathi and Cytryn, 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Baquero et al., 2009 and Tripathi and Cytryn, 2017.

claim: Most natural aminoglycosides are produced by two bacteria genera, Streptomyces and Micromonospora.
source: Also, most natural aminoglycosides are produced by two bacteria genera, Streptomyces and Micromonospora (Durand et al., 2019)⁠, that live mostly in soil and decaying vegetation.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Durand et al., 2019.

claim: Streptomyces and Micromonospora live mostly in soil and decaying vegetation.
source: Also, most natural aminoglycosides are produced by two bacteria genera, Streptomyces and Micromonospora (Durand et al., 2019)⁠, that live mostly in soil and decaying vegetation.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Durand et al., 2019.

claim: Even though 19 times more genomes were sampled in hospitals than in soil, only 2.5 times more CHGs had their first documented occurrence in clinical samples than in soil.
source: Along the same lines, we found that, in our dataset, even though 19 times more genomes were sampled in hospitals than in soil, only 2.5 times more CHGs had their first documented occurrence in clinical samples than in soil.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific ratios comparing sampling and CHG occurrences.

claim: Resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition globally.
source: Previous metagenomic studies using abundance-based metrics found that resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition: either globally (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠, or in specific biomes: soil (Forsberg et al., 2014)⁠, wastewater treatment plants (Ju et al., 2019)⁠, human feces (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition in soil.
source: Previous metagenomic studies using abundance-based metrics found that resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition: either globally (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠, or in specific biomes: soil (Forsberg et al., 2014)⁠, wastewater treatment plants (Ju et al., 2019)⁠, human feces (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Forsberg et al., 2014.

claim: Resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition in wastewater treatment plants.
source: Previous metagenomic studies using abundance-based metrics found that resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition: either globally (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠, or in specific biomes: soil (Forsberg et al., 2014)⁠, wastewater treatment plants (Ju et al., 2019)⁠, human feces (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Ju et al., 2019.

claim: Resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition in human feces.
source: Previous metagenomic studies using abundance-based metrics found that resistome composition is correlated to bacteria community composition: either globally (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠, or in specific biomes: soil (Forsberg et al., 2014)⁠, wastewater treatment plants (Ju et al., 2019)⁠, human feces (Pehrsson et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Pehrsson et al., 2016.

claim: The propagation of AME genes could result from the dissemination of AR bacteria between ecosystems.
source: This correlation indicates that resistome similarity is at least partially due to species composition similarity, and so to the exchange of AR bacteria between biomes. Consequently, our results also indicate that the propagation of AME genes could result from the dissemination of AR bacteria: between ecosystems.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between resistome and species composition.

claim: The propagation could occur by abiotic dissemination, fecal transmission, transmission by wastewater, or transmission through the food chain.
source: The propagation could occur by abiotic dissemination (Allen et al., 2010)⁠, fecal transmission (Karkman et al., 2019)⁠, transmission by wastewater (Vaz-Moreira et al., 2014)⁠, or transmission through the food chain (Founou et al., 2016)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations describing different transmission pathways.

claim: Higher spatial structures increase the likelihood of HGT events to low-abundance strains.
source: Moreover, previous results showed that higher spatial structures increase the likelihood of HGT events to low-abundance strains (Cairns et al., 2018)⁠, that might not be sampled and therefore decrease the likelihood to find a correlation between resistome composition and community composition.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Cairns et al., 2018.

claim: 40% of AME genes are carried by MGEs.
source: In our dataset, 40% of AME genes are carried by MGEs.
evidence: The manuscript provides this specific percentage.

claim: MGE carriage is a strong determinant of the capacity to propagate within and between genome.
source: MGE carriage is known to be a strong determinant of the capacity to propagate within and between genome and has been identified as key element for classifying a given antibiotic resistance in the highest risk category (Martínez et al., 2015)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Martínez et al., 2015.

claim: Half of transposable elements carrying AR genes were also located on plasmids.
source: The association with MGE frequently takes the form of an embedded structure: for example half of transposable elements carrying AR genes were also located on plasmids (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript provides this specific proportion and references Figure 7.

claim: The combination of AME genes within genomes is not random.
source: A second interesting finding is that the combination of AME genes within genomes is not random: the resistance spectrum widens at a higher rate with the number of AME genes than expected by chance, which suggests that the combination of AME genes in a genome is under selection for functional diversification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical analysis of functional diversity.

claim: The combination of AME genes in a genome is under selection for functional diversification.
source: A second interesting finding is that the combination of AME genes within genomes is not random: the resistance spectrum widens at a higher rate with the number of AME genes than expected by chance, which suggests that the combination of AME genes in a genome is under selection for functional diversification.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the non-random pattern of gene combinations.

claim: The broadening of the resistance spectrum is mainly driven by MGEs with inter-genomic mobility.
source: This broadening of the resistance spectrum is mainly driven by MGEs with inter-genomic mobility (i.e. plasmids, ICEs, and prophages).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on analysis of MGE-associated genes.

claim: MGEs increase the likelihood for a genome to carry several copies of the same AR gene.
source: Finally, we also found that MGEs increase the likelihood for a genome to carry several copies of the same AR gene.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on analysis of gene duplications.

claim: The presence of several copies of a resistance gene increases the expression level of AR genes.
source: The presence of several copies of a resistance gene, either because of its association with an intra-genomic MGE or its plasmid carriage not only increases the expression level of AR genes (Depardieu et al., 2007; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009)⁠, but also allows bacteria to evolve new antibiotic resistance functions on duplicated sequences (San Millan and MacLean, 2017; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009)⁠, thus participating in the functional diversification.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Depardieu et al., 2007 and Sandegren and Andersson, 2009.

claim: The presence of several copies of a resistance gene allows bacteria to evolve new antibiotic resistance functions on duplicated sequences.
source: The presence of several copies of a resistance gene, either because of its association with an intra-genomic MGE or its plasmid carriage not only increases the expression level of AR genes (Depardieu et al., 2007; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009)⁠, but also allows bacteria to evolve new antibiotic resistance functions on duplicated sequences (San Millan and MacLean, 2017; Sandegren and Andersson, 2009)⁠, thus participating in the functional diversification.
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to San Millan and MacLean, 2017 and Sandegren and Andersson, 2009.

claim: The screening is likely to underestimate the frequency of resistance carrying genomes because some AME families probably remain unknown.
source: On the one hand, our screening is likely to underestimate the frequency of resistance carrying genomes because some AME families probably remain unknown and aminoglycoside resistance can be conferred by other resistance mechanisms such as target change, hydrolysis, etc. (Blair et al., 2015)⁠.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation and cites Blair et al., 2015.

claim: Aminoglycoside resistance can be conferred by other resistance mechanisms such as target change and hydrolysis.
source: On the one hand, our screening is likely to underestimate the frequency of resistance carrying genomes because some AME families probably remain unknown and aminoglycoside resistance can be conferred by other resistance mechanisms such as target change, hydrolysis, etc. (Blair et al., 2015)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Blair et al., 2015.

claim: The genotype-phenotype relationship is poorly understood for AR genes in general.
source: So far, the genotype-phenotype relationship is poorly understood for AR genes in general (Hughes and Andersson, 2017)⁠, and particularly for AMEs: a single amino acid change is likely to change the enzyme's target, and even to remove its resistance function (Feldgarden et al., 2019; Zárate et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Hughes and Andersson, 2017, Feldgarden et al., 2019, and Zárate et al., 2018.

claim: A single amino acid change is likely to change the enzyme's target, and even to remove its resistance function.
source: So far, the genotype-phenotype relationship is poorly understood for AR genes in general (Hughes and Andersson, 2017)⁠, and particularly for AMEs: a single amino acid change is likely to change the enzyme's target, and even to remove its resistance function (Feldgarden et al., 2019; Zárate et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to Feldgarden et al., 2019 and Zárate et al., 2018.

claim: Sampling was biased towards industrialized countries and towards phyla and biomes with clinical interest.
source: Other limitations come from the fact that our dataset consists of genome sequences in multiple research projects. Because of this, sampling was biased towards industrialized countries and towards phyla and biomes with clinical interest (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for a full overview).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation and references a figure.

claim: The genomes available are not representative of the species composition of the different biomes.
source: Thus, the genomes available are not representative of the species composition of the different biomes and some of the biomes or geographical location are over-represented.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation.

claim: The frequencies of resistant bacteria established in this study are useful for comparisons between biomes, geographical location and time periods but cannot be taken as absolute estimates.
source: The frequencies of resistant bacteria established in this study are useful for comparisons between biomes, geographical location and time periods but cannot be taken as absolute estimates.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation of the data.

claim: Metagenomic studies have shown that AG resistance have evolved in polar communities.
source: Along the same line, the absence of detected resistance in certain places in our data set is likely due to a lack of published genomic data from these places: for example, we did not detect any AME gene in genomes of bacteria from the Antarctic, when metagenomic studies have shown that AG resistance have evolved in polar communities (Perron et al., 2015)⁠.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to Perron et al., 2015.

claim: The main conclusions of the study still hold on each of the subsets analyzed to account for sampling bias.
source: However, the repetition of the analyses on several subsets of the dataset to take sampling bias into account showed that our main conclusions still hold on each of the subsets.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from sensitivity analyses.

claim: Interventional strategies based on reducing antibiotic use should be complemented by a stronger control of exchanges, especially between ecosystems.
source: Together, these results support the idea that interventional strategies based on reducing antibiotic use should be complemented by a stronger control of exchanges, especially between ecosystems.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Understanding the big picture on AR will require a stronger sampling effort in natural ecosystems.
source: Understanding the big picture on AR will require a stronger sampling effort in natural ecosystems and as we have shown that resistomes tend to cluster by ecology rather than by geography, emphasis should be put on monitoring the resistome of all biomes with equal intensity.
evidence: This is a recommendation drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Emphasis should be put on monitoring the resistome of all biomes with equal intensity.
source: Understanding the big picture on AR will require a stronger sampling effort in natural ecosystems and as we have shown that resistomes tend to cluster by ecology rather than by geography, emphasis should be put on monitoring the resistome of all biomes with equal intensity.
evidence: This is a recommendation drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The methods implemented in this study could easily be applied to other AR gene families.
source: Although the conclusions of this study cannot be extended to AR genes other than AMEs, the methods implemented could easily be applied to other AR gene families (especially modifying enzymes).
evidence: The manuscript suggests this as a future direction.

claim: The strong correlation between resistome composition and species composition suggests that AME genes are spreading by AME bacteria between biomes.
source: MGEs are known to be vehicles of HGT and are likely to participate in the spread of AME genes but the strong correlation between resistome composition and species composition established here within biome groups suggests that AME genes are also spreading by AME bacteria between biomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: The relative contributions of HGT and bacteria migration to AR propagation should be investigated on large, integrative datasets.
source: The relative contributions of HGT and bacteria migration to AR propagation as well as the factors that shape and orient them should be investigated on large, integrative datasets in order to understand the antibiotic resistance traffic rules.
evidence: The manuscript suggests this as a future research direction.

claim: 204 sequences of aminoglycoside modifying enzymes were gathered from examples reviewed in Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010 and Garneau-Tsodikova and Labby, 2016.
source: 204 sequences of aminoglycoside modifying enzymes were gathered from examples reviewed in Ramirez and Tolmasky, 2010⁠ and Garneau-Tsodikova and Labby, 2016⁠.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the source of sequences used.

claim: Sequences were grouped in 29 clusters of homologous genes using SiLiX with at least 70% overlap and 35% identity.
source: All the other sequences (Source data 4) were grouped in 29 clusters of homologous genes (CHGs) using SiLiX (v. 1.2.9, Miele et al., 2011)⁠ with the following parameter values: at least 70% overlap and 35% identity to accept BLAST hits for building families.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the clustering methodology.

claim: The genomes included in this study are all the Eubacteria genomes available in the NCBI Refseq database on August 18, 2019.
source: The genomes included in this study are all the Eubacteria genomes available in the NCBI Refseq database on August 18, 2019 and that could be assigned at the species taxonomic level, to the taxonomy bac120 (release 89, Parks et al., 2018)⁠ with the pipeline GTDB-tk (v. 1.0.2, Chaumeil et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the genome dataset.

claim: Around 1,200,000 hits were found in the 160,987 genomes screened.
source: The genomes were screened for the presence of the 29 CHG profiles defined using the hmmsearch command of HMMER (v. 3.3). Around 1,200,000 hits were found in the 160,987 genomes screened.
evidence: The Materials and methods section provides the number of initial hits.

claim: Results were kept with cutoff values of 10–3 for e-value and 0.95 for accuracy.
source: Results were kept with cutoff values of 10–3 for e-value and 0.95 for accuracy, and if the length of the predicted proteins was at least 80% of the one of the corresponding profile.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the filtering criteria.
